lead: A wire radiates when the charges in it accelerate. A current that changes in time sends out a field that keeps travelling at the speed of light, falls as 1/r and carries power to any distance: that is radiation. The simplest radiator is the Hertzian dipole, a current element much shorter than a wavelength with the same current all along it. Its fields follow from the retarded vector potential, and every wire antenna is a sum of such elements.
prereq: You need: Maxwell’s equations in phasor form and the plane wave in free space, with intrinsic impedance η = 120π ≈ 377 Ω and phase constant β = 2π/λ.

blocks.text: A charge moving at steady speed carries its field lines with it and nothing leaves. When it speeds up or slows down, the distant parts of its field cannot learn of the change at once, because news travels at c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s. A kink forms between the old field and the new one and runs outward as a wave: that detached field is radiation.

In a wire of length l, l dI/dt = q dv/dt: a changing current is accelerating charge. A steady (DC) current does not radiate. Switching it off abruptly is a sudden deceleration and launches a short pulse, as in a spark-gap transmitter; a sinusoidal current accelerates its charges all the time, so it radiates all the time.

On a two-wire line the currents in the two close wires are opposite, so their fields cancel at a distance. Bend the last quarter wavelength of each wire outwards until they are in line: the two currents now point the same way, their fields add, and the open line has become a half-wave dipole.

The magnetic vector potential A at a point P sums every bit of current in the antenna, each taken as it was R/c seconds earlier, R being its distance from P; hence “retarded”. In phasor form the delay is the factor e<sup>−jβR</sup>.
A = (μ₀/4π) ∫ J e−jβR / R dV′. Here J is the current density in A/m² at the source point, dV′ the source volume element, R the source-to-point distance in m and μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m

Once A is known, the fields follow: H = (1/μ₀) ∇ × A, and away from the source E comes from Maxwell’s equation E = (1/jωε₀) ∇ × H, with ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m and ω = 2πf. Some syllabi also use the electric vector potential F = (ε₀/4π) ∫ M e−jβR/R dV′, built from a magnetic current density M, for slots and apertures. The route is always current → A → H → E.
Put an element of length l ≪ λ at the origin along z, carrying a uniform peak current I₀. In spherical coordinates r is the distance, θ the angle from the wire and φ the angle round it.

items: Since l ≪ r, every part of the element is at R ≈ r, so the integral collapses to A<sub>z</sub> = μ₀ I₀ l e<sup>−jβr</sup> / (4πr).
Resolve A<sub>z</sub> into spherical parts: A<sub>r</sub> = A<sub>z</sub> cos θ and A<sub>θ</sub> = −A<sub>z</sub> sin θ.
The curl gives one magnetic component: H<sub>φ</sub> = j β I₀ l sin θ e<sup>−jβr</sup> / (4πr) × [1 + 1/(jβr)].

Then E = (1/jωε₀) ∇ × H gives two electric components: E<sub>r</sub> = η I₀ l cos θ e<sup>−jβr</sup> / (2πr²) × [1 + 1/(jβr)] and E<sub>θ</sub> = j η β I₀ l sin θ e<sup>−jβr</sup> / (4πr) × [1 + 1/(jβr) − 1/(βr)²].

blocks.text: The brackets hold terms in 1/r, 1/r² and 1/r³. The 1/r³ (electrostatic) and 1/r² (induction) terms store energy; the 1/r term is the radiation field. All three are equal at βr = 1, that is r = λ/2π.

Far away (βr ≫ 1) only the 1/r terms are left, Er vanishes and the far field is Eθ = j η β I₀ l sin θ e−jβr / (4πr), with Hφ = Eθ/η. Using ηβ/4π = 30β = 60π/λ, the magnitude is |Eθ| = 60π I₀ l sin θ / (λ r). E ⊥ H ⊥ r with E/H = η: locally a plane wave. The pattern is sin θ: zero along the wire, largest broadside, the same at every φ.
The average power density is S = |E<sub>θ</sub>|²/(2η) W/m². Integrating it over a sphere of radius r, using the integral of sin³θ from 0 to π, which is 4/3, gives
Prad = 40π² (I₀ l/λ)² W. The r cancels, as it must: the same power crosses every sphere

Defining the radiation resistance Rr by Prad = ½ I₀² Rr gives Rr = 80π² (l/λ)² Ω. This holds for uniform current; a real short dipole, whose current falls linearly to zero at the tips, has one quarter of it, 20π²(l/λ)². The sin²θ power pattern has directivity 1.5.

figure.caption: The worked example’s 1 cm element at 1 GHz, drawn in a plane through the wire: the far field is 62.8 sin θ mV/m at 100 m, so it is largest broadside, half as large at θ = 30° and zero along the wire.

spec.aria: Polar plot of the field of a short vertical current element: two circles touching at the element, widest to the left and right. The point at 90 degrees is marked 62.8 millivolts per metre and the point at 30 degrees 31.4. A side panel lists l = 1 cm, 1 GHz, radiation resistance 0.877 ohm and radiated power 0.439 watt.

examples.question: A Hertzian dipole of length l = 1 cm carries a uniform peak current I₀ = 1 A at f = 1 GHz. Find (a) l/λ, (b) R<sub>r</sub> and P<sub>rad</sub>, (c) |E<sub>θ</sub>| and |H<sub>φ</sub>| at r = 100 m broadside and at θ = 30°, and (d) check the power density against P<sub>rad</sub> with D = 1.5.
steps: λ = c/f = 3 × 10⁸ / 10⁹ = 0.3 m, so l/λ = 0.01/0.3 = 0.0333: well below 0.1, so the Hertzian model holds.
Broadside, with βr = 2094 ≫ 1 so only the 1/r term matters: |E<sub>θ</sub>| = 60π I₀ l / (λ r) = 60π × 1 × 0.01 / (0.3 × 100) = 0.0628 V/m = 62.8 mV/m.
At θ = 30°: |E<sub>θ</sub>| = 62.8 × sin 30° = 31.4 mV/m, half the broadside value.
Check: S = D P<sub>rad</sub>/(4πr²) = 1.5 × 0.439 / (4π × 100²) = 5.24 × 10⁻⁶ W/m². The two routes agree.
examples.answer: l/λ = 0.0333; R<sub>r</sub> = 0.877 Ω; P<sub>rad</sub> = 0.439 W; |E<sub>θ</sub>| = 62.8 mV/m broadside and 31.4 mV/m at 30°; |H<sub>φ</sub>| = 0.167 mA/m; S = 5.24 µW/m².

examples.question: For the same dipole (λ = 0.3 m), compare the sizes of the three terms 1, 1/(βr) and 1/(βr)² in the E<sub>θ</sub> bracket at r = λ/2π, r = λ and r = 10λ. Where may the 1/r² and 1/r³ terms be dropped?
steps: r = λ/2π = 0.0477 m: βr = 1, so the three terms are 1, 1 and 1; the far-field formula is badly wrong here.
r = λ = 0.3 m: βr = 6.28, so 1/(βr) = 0.159 and 1/(βr)² = 0.0253; the induction term is still 16 per cent.
r = 10λ = 3 m: βr = 62.8, so 1/(βr) = 0.0159 and 1/(βr)² = 0.000253; below 2 per cent, so they can be dropped.
examples.answer: The three terms are equal at r = λ/2π = 4.8 cm; at r = λ the 1/r² term is still 16 %; by r = 10λ = 3 m it is 1.6 % and the far-field formula may be used.

traps: Using R<sub>r</sub> = 80π²(l/λ)² for a short dipole with triangular current. That formula is for uniform current (the Hertzian dipole); a real short dipole gives 20π²(l/λ)², four times less.
Keeping 1/r² or 1/r³ terms in a far-field answer, or dropping them close in. The far field is the 1/r term only, and only once βr ≫ 1.
Drawing the pattern with its maximum along the wire. The sin θ factor makes the axis a null and broadside the maximum.
Using P = I₀² R<sub>r</sub> with a peak current. With peak I₀ the power is ½ I₀² R<sub>r</sub>; the ½ goes only if I is an rms value.

quiz.q: What is meant by a retarded potential?
quiz.a: A potential built from each source current as it was R/c seconds earlier, R being the source-to-point distance; in phasor form the delay is the factor e<sup>−jβR</sup>.

quiz.q: Write the far-field E<sub>θ</sub> and H<sub>φ</sub> of a Hertzian dipole.
quiz.a: E<sub>θ</sub> = jηβI₀ l sin θ e<sup>−jβr</sup>/(4πr) and H<sub>φ</sub> = E<sub>θ</sub>/η, with η = 120π Ω and β = 2π/λ.

quiz.q: Why does a steady current in a straight wire not radiate, while a sinusoidal current does?
quiz.a: Radiation needs accelerating charge, and l dI/dt = q dv/dt. A steady current has dI/dt = 0, so its field stays tied to the wire. A sinusoidal current changes all the time, so its charges keep accelerating and launch a travelling field.

quiz.q: At what distance are the 1/r, 1/r² and 1/r³ terms of a Hertzian dipole equal, and why does it matter?
quiz.a: At βr = 1, that is r = λ/2π. Inside it the stored (near) fields dominate; well beyond it only the 1/r radiation field is left, so far-field formulas apply.

quiz.q: A Hertzian dipole has l = 2 mm and I₀ = 2 A at 3 GHz. Find l/λ, R<sub>r</sub> and |E<sub>θ</sub>| at 50 m broadside.
Show that the radiated power of a Hertzian dipole does not depend on the radius of the sphere used to compute it.
quiz.a: S = |E<sub>θ</sub>|²/(2η) varies as 1/r², while the sphere area 4πr² grows as r². Their product, P<sub>rad</sub> = 40π²(I₀ l/λ)², has no r, so the same power crosses every sphere: it has left for good.

beyond: Not for the exam. Full-wave solvers (method of moments, FDTD) evaluate the same retarded-potential integral over thousands of small current segments; that is how phone and car antennas are designed. Search next for “method of moments wire antenna” and “Larmor formula”.
